MA3491 overview

MA3491 Topic Guide

Hamming Codes over Finite Fields

Projectively distinct nonzero columns in H make each single-symbol error announce its position and magnitude.

Purpose

Hamming codes are a compact construction of perfect single-error-correcting q-ary codes.Exam use: Definition, parameters, column convention, syndrome arithmetic, correction, parity recheck and perfect-code count appear.

Question plan

  1. Set n=(qr−1)/(q−1) and k=n−r.
  2. Make H from one representative of each one-dimensional subspace of Fqr.
  3. Use C=ker H; row-reduce H to derive a G if requested.
  4. Decode a one-error word from its syndrome: identify the column and, when q>2, the nonzero error magnitude.
  5. Question interpretation: For binary codes, use each nonzero r-bit column once. For general q, use no zero column and no two scalar-multiple columns; for perfect, verify the q-ary radius-one sphere count.

Formulas

Hamming code Ham(r,q): [n,n−r,3], where n=(qr−1)/(q−1). It has qn−r words and t=1; sphere packing is an equality. Its check-matrix columns are one representative from each one-dimensional subspace of Fqr.Rapid recall: for q=2 this becomes [2r−1,2r−1−r,3]; in general, correct a syndrome by matching it to a nonzero scalar multiple of a column.

Derivation

No column of H is zero and no two columns are scalar multiples, so a nonzero codeword cannot have weight 1 or 2; d≥3. An error of nonzero magnitude a in coordinate i has syndrome a times column i, so its position and magnitude are determined. Counting gives qn−r(1+n(q−1))=qn, hence perfect and d=3.Exam workflow: Freeze the column convention, derive G in systematic form if requested, calculate the syndrome in Fq, correct the matching coordinate/magnitude, and check Hc^T=0.

Worked example

For m=3, n=7. Take H with columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111. A syndrome 101 points to position 5, so flip bit 5.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

For m=3 choose H columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111. If r=1101000, syndrome is 001 xor 010 xor 100=111, so flip bit 7 to get c=1101001. Recheck: 001 xor 010 xor 100 xor 111=000. The [7,4,3] code has 16 codewords and ball size 8, giving 16*8=128=2^7, hence perfect.

Graduated exam bridge

1. Give [n,k,d] for m=4. Check: [15,11,3].

2. Construct H for m=3, prove it corrects one error, and verify the sphere-packing equality. Check: include both distinct-column and counting arguments.

Hard paper-style synthesis

Paper-style synthesis: prove d_min=3 from the columns of H. Check no zero column rules out weight 1 and no repeated columns rules out weight 2; columns 001 xor 010 xor 011=0 exhibit a weight-3 codeword.

Practice question - Hamming correction and perfection [8 marks]

Inspired by: MA3491 2024/25 Q4(a-e). Task. For Ham(3,2) with all nonzero 3-bit H columns, explain one-error correction and verify perfection. [8 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use distinct nonzero syndromes for correction and the sphere count for perfection.

Worked answer: H has n=23-1=7 columns, each a different nonzero vector of F23. An error in coordinate i has syndrome HeiT, precisely column i; distinct columns identify the one flipped bit. The code has parameters [7,4,3], so 24=16 codewords and radius t=1. Each radius-one ball has 1+7=8 words. Thus 16·8=128=27, so the balls exactly partition the ambient space and the code is perfect.

Topic-specific trap: a zero syndrome means no error only under the at-most-one-error model.

Mistakes

  • Including the zero column.
  • Using n=2m rather than 2m−1.
  • Reading syndrome bits in a different order from H.
  • Recovery rule: The binary value of a syndrome names a bit only if the column ordering uses that convention; otherwise locate the matching column directly.

Checklist

  • I can build H.
  • I can recover n and k.
  • I can explain perfect single-error correction.
  • Final 60-second audit: Parameters, column convention, syndrome arithmetic, flipped bit, parity recheck and perfect-code count appear.
